transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-26
Time: 10:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Quantaco Head of MLOps), Priya Singh (Product), Carlos Mendez (Infra)

[00:00] Jordan Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate the time. This is Jordan from Redwood, and Maya is with me — SE lead. Quick check, audio okay?
[00:10] Liam O'Connor: Yep, all good.
[00:12] Priya Singh: Good here.
[00:15] Jordan Patel: Great. Goal today is to review the last week's POC numbers, focus on cost/unit economics — tokens per second per dollar, caching impact, and batching tradeoffs — and agree next steps for the production pilot.

[01:05] Maya Chen: I'll start with a quick recap of the benchmark we ran Friday. We ran model A (open-llama-64q) and model B (redwood-7B-8bit) across three batching profiles and with/without prefix/KV caching. Automatic batching was at sizes 16, 32, 64 — those are logical batch sizes, not GPU-specific limits.
[01:35] Carlos Mendez: Quick q, when you say prefix caching you mean the KV cache for repeated prompt prefixes?
[01:40] Maya Chen: Yeah, exactly. We used prefix-level KV caching and also tested a small request-level cache for deterministic prompts. Hit rates varied depending on the prompt set.

[02:05] Priya Singh: Can you remind us how tokens/sec/$ is calculated here? I want to make sure we match our finance model.
[02:12] Jordan Patel: Sure. We took total generated tokens over the run divided by total GPU cost for the same run window. For hosted numbers we used Redwood hosted list price equivalent, for dedicated we used a modeled AWS GPU hourly rate plus infra overhead. So tokens per dollar is tokens / (gpu_hour_cost * hours). We kept p95 latency target ~300ms for production sim.

[03:00] Maya Chen: Results: model B with 8-bit quant and prefix caching gave the best tokens/sec/$ in our tests — about 1.8x improvement over the non-quant baseline when caching hit-rate was ~40%. With higher cache hits (60–70%) we saw up to 2.5x. Batching increases throughput but increases tail latency; at batch 64 average tokens/sec rose 2.2x vs batch 16 but p95 latency jumped from 280ms to 620ms, so tradeoff there.

[04:15] Liam O'Connor: That's helpful. Our SLO for interactive features is p95 < 400ms, so batch 64 is out for low-latency endpoints. But for async summarization we can tolerate higher latency.

[04:40] Maya Chen: Right. So suggestion: route interactive calls to lower batch windows and use aggressive prefix caching and request-level caching for deterministic prompts. Route long-running jobs to larger batch profiles to amortize cost.

[05:20] Carlos Mendez: On Dedicated vs Hosted — how different were the cost models? We have internal constraints on data residency and egress.
[05:27] Jordan Patel: For hosted, you get simpler ops and economies of scale; tokens/sec/$ we measured for hosted was similar to dedicated when utilization is >70%. Dedicated has a higher fixed cost but predictable throughput and gives you control over VPC and KMS. For low QPS with big peaks, burst capacity and autoscaling matter — Dedicated can be cheaper if you can fill reserved capacity.

[06:05] Priya Singh: Any notes on quantization accuracy/regressions? Our QA is sensitive to hallucination rate.
[06:12] Maya Chen: We ran quality regressions with the same eval set — model B in 8-bit had minor score drift on abstractive tasks, mostly in longer context hallucination, but within acceptable bounds for your use-case (ranking + assistant style). We can run a selective post-quantization calibration with a few hundred eval prompts which reduces drift.

[07:00] Liam O'Connor: What's the expected cache-hit rates in production? Our product has a lot of repeated boilerplate prompts but also many unique user inputs.
[07:08] Maya Chen: Based on your sample logs, we estimate 30–45% prefix cache hit for the assistant flows and request-level caching maybe 10–15% for common templates. If you standardize some prompt templates you can push that higher.

[08:05] Jordan Patel: Important note: caching reduces compute but not egress if you need to send full context externally. For Private deployments egress is less of a concern.

[08:30] Carlos Mendez: We will likely go Private or Dedicated because of residency and KMS requirements. For Dedicated, what's the expected tokens/sec/$ when using GPUs similar to p4d but with 8-bit quant?
[08:40] Maya Chen: Our modeled numbers for a p4d-like instance with 8-bit quant and prefix caching at 40% were about 3.5M tokens per hour per GPU which we translate to tokens/sec/$ of roughly 14k tokens/sec per dollar across the instance hour economics — these are model- and workload-dependent. We'll share the spreadsheet with exact assumptions.

[09:30] Priya Singh: Could you also show the delta for NVMe caching vs in-memory KV? Our infra team cares about memory footprint.
[09:38] Maya Chen: We didn't test NVMe in this run. NVMe-backed KV helps for very large working sets but adds latency — it's a fallback. For most of your patterns in the sample prompts, in-memory KV is enough and lower latency. We'll note NVMe as a follow-up test if you expect >1TB KV state.

[10:20] Liam O'Connor: There was mention of automatic fallback policies earlier — can you remind how Redwood handles model fallbacks to keep apps online during capacity spikes?
[10:28] Jordan Patel: Sure — Smart routing can fallback to smaller model variants (e.g., from redwood-13B to 7B quant) or fall back to hosted pool in another region. Fallbacks prioritize preserving latency SLOs; quality impact is captured in A/B eval. We can configure per-route policies.

[11:05] Carlos Mendez: Any billing surprises around request-level caching? Do you still pay for tokens if you hit a cache?
[11:12] Jordan Patel: For caching hits we don't re-run the model so compute cost is avoided. Billing depends on contract: hosted API charges reflect served tokens; for Dedicated you pay for the underlying capacity whether used or not, so effective tokens/$ depends on utilization. We'll call that out in the spreadsheet.

[12:00] Maya Chen: Quick demo note: we instrumented token-level tracing so you can see which prefixes hit cache and which requests caused new model work — sharing a sample trace link in Slack after this.

[13:10] Priya Singh: On batching tradeoffs, if we target p95 < 400ms for interactive, what's a safe batch size?
[13:18] Maya Chen: For your prompt lengths (median 120 tokens), batch 16 gives p95 ~320–350ms in our run. Batch 32 pushes p95 close to 480–520ms. So recommended default interactive batch=16, adaptive batching to expand when load is low, and strict tail-latency guardrails.

[14:00] Liam O'Connor: Do you support dynamic batching per route? We want different endpoints with different SLOs.
[14:05] Jordan Patel: Yes, per-route batching profiles are supported; the console will let you set min/max batch and latency objectives.

[15:00] Maya Chen: We also tested pinned KV caches per customer session. That boosted effective cache hit for repeated multi-turn flows — helpful for agent-like sessions where earlier context repeats.

[16:00] Carlos Mendez: Network egress: do you have numbers for data transfer cost differences between Hosted and Dedicated in us-east-1? We have to model egress for billing to customers.

[16:12] Jordan Patel: We'll add egress assumptions to the spreadsheet. Hosted includes egress charges in our public pricing notes, but Dedicated egress is per-cloud billing — so we model it separately.

[17:00] Priya Singh: For the 1M token benchmark Maya will run, what variants should be included?
[17:07] Maya Chen: We'll include redwood-7B 8-bit, redwood-13B 8-bit, open-llama baseline (float), and a quantized 4-bit path if you want to test lower-precision. Also with/without prefix caching and three batching profiles.

[18:00] Liam O'Connor: We're also tracking quality regression thresholds; if quant causes >3% drop on our eval metric we need to flag. Can you include that in the results?
[18:08] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll include eval deltas and a recommendations column.

[19:00] Jordan Patel: Quick run-of show: Jordan to send spreadsheet, Maya to run benchmark, Quantaco sends prompts. Then we'll reconvene next week to review numbers and discuss Dedicated sizing.

[20:15] Priya Singh: Any compliance/security blockers we should be aware of for Dedicated?
[20:22] Jordan Patel: Dedicated gives you VPC, SAML/SSO, and integrates with KMS/HSM for keys. We also provide audit logs and can sign BAA/SOC2 addenda. We've already shared the security pack; please flag any open items.

[21:05] Carlos Mendez: One small thing — latency stability over time during garbage collection/eviction. Did you see any jitter during the long runs?
[21:12] Maya Chen: We saw sporadic spikes when we warmed a cold KV store; with warm start and proper prefetching it's stable. We'll include jitter graphs in the run artifacts.

[22:30] Liam O'Connor: On cost math — if we move more of the workload to cached responses and also split async jobs to large batches, what's the ballpark reduction in monthly bill?
[22:38] Jordan Patel: With conservative assumptions (40% cache hit, 50% of workload batched async), we estimate a 30–45% reduction in compute cost vs naive no-cache no-batching baseline. We'll show a sensitivity table in the doc.

[24:00] Priya Singh: Anything else from the Redwood side?
[24:05] Maya Chen: We'll also run a Dedicated scale test to validate autoscaler behavior at burst — simulating 3x expected peak for 30 minutes. Good to confirm how reserved capacity and burst interacts.

[25:00] Jordan Patel: Ok let's recap next steps —
[25:05] Jordan Patel: 1) Jordan share spreadsheet with tokens/sec/$, egress and assumptions.
[25:10] Jordan Patel: 2) Maya run 1M token benchmark with outlined variants and caching/batching profiles.
[25:18] Jordan Patel: 3) Quantaco shares final prompt set and QPS targets.
[25:22] Jordan Patel: 4) Schedule Dedicated sizing deep-dive for Sept 7.

[26:00] Carlos Mendez: Sounds good. I'll send the prompt set and constraints by end of week.

[26:45] Priya Singh: Quick question — will you require full data access to run these tests? We're sending anonymized prompts, not PII.
[26:52] Maya Chen: No PII required, anonymized prompts are fine. For Private we can discuss connectivity options if you want us to run on-prem.

[28:00] Liam O'Connor: One more ask — can you surface a simple per-endpoint cost estimate in the Console? Product would like to show an estimate for feature owners.
[28:08] Jordan Patel: There's a cost estimator in Console beta; we'll enable a per-route breakdown for you and show how tokens map to charges. I'll add that to the spreadsheet notes.

[30:00] Maya Chen: I'll post links to the traces and the initial run artifacts in the shared Confluence page after the call.

[31:00] Priya Singh: Great. Any risks we should call out?

[31:05] Jordan Patel: Main risks: quantization quality regressions on certain long-form tasks, and utilization variance for Dedicated that affects effective tokens/$ if capacity is underutilized. Mitigations: calibration suite, adaptive batching, and start with a small reserved footprint plus burst.

[33:00] Liam O'Connor: Timeline question — if POC metrics look good, how long to get Dedicated up and running?

[33:08] Jordan Patel: Typically 4–6 weeks for Dedicated provisioning after contract, including network setup and KMS onboarding. Private on-prem can take longer depending on approvals.

[34:30] Carlos Mendez: On the calibration for quant, will that be done by Redwood or we run locally?

[34:36] Maya Chen: We can run calibration runs for you on our infra or hand over a small toolkit to run in your Dedicated environment. Depends on preference.

[36:00] Priya Singh: Any open security questionnaire items?

[36:05] Jordan Patel: We answered most; Carlos flagged a specific SOC2 evidence item — we're following up with our security team and will share logs.

[37:00] Liam O'Connor: Ok I'm satisfied — looks actionable.

[37:10] Jordan Patel: Great. We'll get the artifacts out today and target the benchmark by next Tuesday.

[38:00] Priya Singh: Thanks team.

[38:05] Carlos Mendez: Thanks.

[38:10] Jordan Patel: Thanks all. We'll follow up in Slack with the spreadsheet and links.

[44:30] (meeting end)

Notes: transcript contains some auto-transcription errors and speaker label drift — e.g., 'redwood inferencing' appears instead of 'Redwood Inference' in a few lines. Action items summarized above.
